Museum Copy And Harbour Model · Reading

A museum placed a copy of an old bowl on a table where visitors could examine its shape more closely. Some people were pleased; others thought that a copy had no place beside original objects. The curator asked what each object was being used to explain. ____1____ The copy and the original did not have to answer exactly the same question.

The original carried marks from its own history. Its surface could provide evidence of use, repair and change. ____2____ A newly made version could reproduce a shape without having undergone those experiences.

The copy nevertheless allowed a different kind of access. Visitors could turn it to see parts difficult to view in the case. ____3____ The activity made sense when its purpose was clear, not when the object was presented as something it was not.

The museum made the label visible from every side of the table. ____4____ A visitor arriving halfway through a demonstration should not have to guess whether the bowl was old or newly made.

The discussion changed the way the team planned later displays. ____5____ The question was how a material, a label and an activity worked together to support a particular understanding.

Museum Copy And Harbour Model · Grammar

A visitor centre asked our class to help explain a model of an old harbour. Several parts ____1____ (REBUILD) since the model was first displayed, and the label needed to make that history clear. The teacher asked us ____2____ (COMPARE) the current version with earlier photographs.

The model, ____3____ maker had kept a notebook, was not simply a smaller version of everything that had existed. Some details had been simplified so visitors could see the main layout. We needed to explain ____4____ those choices affected the way the model should be read.

After ____5____ (EXAMINE) the notes, we wrote a caption distinguishing the original work from later additions. The caption was ____6____ (PRECISE) than our first draft because it avoided treating every visible feature as equally old.

The maker suggested ____7____ (KEEP) one earlier photograph beside the model. That would help visitors notice the change without having to imagine it from a sentence alone. He also said that a short explanation could not replace every possible question.

The final label ____8____ (READ) by the staff before printing. We described its limits ____9____ (CLEAR), and the process helped ____10____ (WE) understand why a model could remain useful while being revised.

Volunteer Titles And School Guests · Reading

At a volunteer festival, the organisers called one role “team leader”. Several new helpers assumed that the person wearing that badge must know how to answer every question. In fact, some leaders were responsible mainly for keeping a rota and finding the appropriate contact. ____1____ A title could describe a task without claiming unlimited expertise.

A school charity report announced that volunteers had collected eighty boxes of books. The number sounded impressive, but a pupil asked how many books the boxes contained. Some were large and full; others held only a few heavy volumes. ____1____ The same box count could describe quite different amounts of material.

The organisers did not remove the original total. It was still a useful record of the transport task. ____2____ A count of containers answered a different question from a count of the objects inside them.

For the next collection, volunteers recorded both figures. They also marked boxes that contained mixed material, such as books and magazines. ____3____ A total needed a clear definition of what was being counted.

The final report explained the method beside the numbers rather than hiding it in a note nobody would notice. ____4____ Readers should be able to understand the basis of a comparison before using it to judge whether the collection had grown.

The group was still proud of the work. ____5____ A more careful account allowed that pride to rest on information that other people could interpret.

Our class helped prepare a programme for the town theatre's anniversary. Before choosing any quotations, the teacher ____1____ (ASK) us to identify the speaker and the occasion for each line. A sentence could sound more definite ____2____ its author had intended when it was removed from a longer speech.

Debate Definitions And Cycle Route · Reading

In a class debate about a proposed cycle lane, two groups appeared to disagree about everything. One said the route was convenient; the other said it was not. The teacher asked what each group meant by convenient. ____1____ One had considered a direct journey to school, while the other had focused on places to leave a bicycle.

We wrote the two meanings separately before continuing. ____2____ The groups could then see that one statement did not directly answer the other, even though both used the same adjective.

This did not make all disagreement disappear. Some differences remained after the terms were clear. ____3____ Shared wording made the remaining dispute more precise rather than forcing everyone to reach the same conclusion.

We also distinguished a fact that needed checking from a preference that people might reasonably hold differently. ____4____ The number of parking spaces could be investigated; how much someone valued a shorter route was not simply a wrong number.

The final summary recorded both points of agreement and reasons for continuing disagreement. ____5____ A useful discussion had become possible because the groups had stopped assuming that the same word guaranteed the same question.

The planner, ____3____ comments we had read, separated the route surface from the place where riders crossed a road. Both mattered, but one figure could not answer every question. We needed to identify ____4____ part of the route a claim concerned.

After ____5____ (COMPARE) our notes, we found one statement based on an outdated map. It ____6____ (CORRECT) before we returned to the discussion. The correction did not automatically settle a separate question about convenience.

Had we treated the first figure as a complete answer, we ____7____ (OVERLOOK) that difference. The teacher encouraged us to describe the evidence ____8____ (PRECISE) and say which points remained matters of judgement.

Our final summary was more ____9____ (BALANCE) than the first draft. It helped ____10____ (WE) see that a clear disagreement could be more useful than an apparent agreement built on different meanings.

Hotel Status And Timetable Periods · Reading

At a training session for a small hotel, new staff were asked what the word “available” meant on a room board. One person said that no guest was inside. Another said that the room was ready for the next arrival. ____1____ An empty room might still be waiting for cleaning or a final check.

The manager used separate status cards for departure, preparation and readiness. ____2____ Each card described a stage in the work rather than inviting every person to supply their own meaning.

Updating the board was part of the task, not a favour to the next shift. ____3____ A completed check that remained only in one person's memory could leave colleagues acting on an earlier state.

The team also agreed how to report an unexpected delay. Staff did not need to announce a reason to every waiting guest, but the relevant colleague needed enough information to respond. ____4____ Keeping a message short was not the same as leaving out the part that explained what could happen next.

The training ended with a simple changeover exercise. ____5____ When two cards seemed to disagree, staff practised asking which stage had actually been completed instead of deciding that the board was useless.

During our visit to a seaside town, the station displayed two timetables for the same route. One ____1____ (REPLACE) the following week, but both remained visible while staff prepared the change. The teacher asked us ____2____ (CHECK) the date before choosing a departure.

A station worker, ____3____ explanation we needed, showed us how the period of use was printed above each list. A number could be correct on one timetable and still be ____4____ (SUITABLE) for our journey that day.

Instead of ____5____ (ASSUME) that the newest-looking sheet was the current one, we read the heading. This made the choice easier ____6____ (EXPLAIN) to another member of the group. Appearance alone had not established which times applied.

Had we followed the wrong sheet, we ____7____ (ARRIVE) after the intended train had left. We wrote the applicable date beside the departure in our notes and checked the platform separately.

The return plan ____8____ (REVIEW) before we left the town centre. We described the change ____9____ (CLEAR) so that everyone could understand ____10____ (WE) arrangement without having been present for the worker's explanation.

Support After Match And Coach Interview · Reading

After losing a school badminton match, I expected my friend to tell me that I should have won. Instead, she asked whether I wanted to talk about the game or leave it for later. ____1____ Her question gave me a choice before turning my disappointment into a discussion.

When I said I wanted to talk, she began with what I had found difficult. I mentioned the short returns that had drawn me towards the net. ____2____ We could discuss a part of the game instead of arguing about whether the whole afternoon was a success or a failure.

She did not promise that one adjustment would guarantee a win next time. She suggested a short practice and offered to help me try it. ____3____ The offer concerned something we could do, not a result neither of us controlled.

At the next practice, I still made mistakes. My friend asked what had changed and what remained difficult. ____4____ Improvement did not have to mean that the problem had disappeared in a single session.

I remembered the conversation because it had made me feel supported without asking me to pretend that I was no longer disappointed. ____5____ An honest response and a practical next step had mattered more than an easy claim that the result should have been different.

The coach, ____3____ first club had used an outdoor court, described how practice arrangements had changed. He said that a session could be useful even ____4____ it did not produce an immediate improvement in results.

After ____5____ (LISTEN) to the recording, we separated his advice from our own summary. One sentence ____6____ (QUOTE) without a qualifying phrase in our first draft. Restoring the phrase made the meaning more ____7____ (ACCURACY).

We also asked whether the same advice would ____8____ (APPLY) to a beginner. The coach explained that a suggestion needed to be understood in relation to the person and the task. We described that limit ____9____ (EXPLICIT) in the final article.

The project helped ____10____ (WE) see why a good interview involved following an answer, not merely reaching the end of prepared questions.

Diary Voices And Traveller Letter · Reading

A class creating an audio guide recorded a student reading an old diary. At the first rehearsal, listeners thought the speaker had personally experienced the events. The team had introduced the date but had not explained that the words were being performed. ____1____ Knowing when a text was written did not establish who was speaking in the recording.

The revised introduction named the diary writer and the reader separately. ____2____ Listeners could then connect the historical account with its source without confusing it with a present-day memory.

The students also noticed that the reader's pauses could make a sentence sound doubtful or certain. ____3____ The words remained the same, but the performance contributed to the impression a listener received.

They tried a second reading and compared the effects. Rather than claiming that one version contained no interpretation, they explained the choice they had made. ____4____ The guide could acknowledge a decision without turning every brief extract into a lecture.

At the exhibition, the diary extract appeared alongside its introduction and source note. ____5____ Visitors heard an engaging voice while still being able to distinguish the record from the way it had been presented.

The student, ____3____ voice we recorded, practised the passage twice. We discussed ____4____ the pauses might affect a listener's understanding, comparing a hesitant delivery with a confident one.

After ____5____ (HEAR) both versions, we chose the less dramatic reading. We did not claim it was completely free of interpretation. The source note ____6____ (INCLUDE) in the final display so that visitors could find the original letter.

Had we omitted the introduction, some listeners ____7____ (MISTAKE) the performance for a personal recollection. We described the recording ____8____ (ACCURATE) as a reading rather than an interview.

The final arrangement was more ____9____ (INFORM) than the first draft. It helped ____10____ (WE) see how a clear introduction could support an engaging presentation.
